la:verb:careo.gloss: to lack, be without. (usually with ablative), to be deprived of
senses: to lack, be without. (usually with ablative), to be deprived of
la:verb:careo.html:
căreo, ui, ĭtum (carĭtūrus, ; ; ; ; ; ; .—
Part. pr. gen. plur. carentum, ; ; ), 2 (pres. subj. carint = careant, .— Dep. form careor, acc. to Caper ap. P.), v. n.
cf. κείρω, καρῆναι; Germ. scheeren; Engl. shear
, to be cut off from, be without, to want, be in want of, not to have, whether in a good or bad sense; but κατʼ ἐξοχήν, to be devoid of, to want, to be without some good; and with reference to the subjective state of mind, to miss it (accordingly, of a good that is merely desirable, while egere is used of the want of that which is necessary); constr. regularly with abl.; in ante-class. poets also with gen. or acc. (the latter also in late Lat.).
To be without, devoid of, not to have, to be free from (corresp. with abesse, ; and opp. frui,).
Of living subjects: carere culpā,; : calumniā,: malis,: dolore,; : febri,, and by poet. license with an inverted construction: caruitne febris te heri?: morbis,: malo,: suspicione,; : vitiis,; ; : stultitiā,: ambitione,: appellatione,: omnibus his quasi morbis voluit carere sapientem,: calumniā,: conspiratione et periculo,: stultitiae atque ignorantiae crimine, Auct. B. G. 8 praef.: communi sensu,: morte,to be immortal,; : suis figurā,; cf. of virtue, personified: culpāque omni carens praeter se ipsam nihil censet ad se pertinere,.—
To be without a thing from free-will, i.e. to deprive one's self of a thing

not to make use of it, to deny one's self a thing, to abstain from (syn.: abstineo, absum; hence opp. utor; v.the foll.): temeto,; Fragm. ap. ; cf. vino,: nec Veneris fructu,renounces not.: lubidinibus,: amicorum facultatibus,: mulieribus facile,; cf. absol.: satiatis vero et expletis jucundius est carere quam frui,.—With acc.: Tandem non ego illam caream, ei sit opus, vel totum triduom?.— Hence,

Of localities, to hold one's self aloof from, not to go to; or merely, to be absent from (cf. abstineo, II.): foro, senatu, publico,; cf.: provinciā domoque,: aspectu civium,: declamationibus nostris,: forensi luce,: patria,; : Roma,.—
Of inanimate subjects: terra caret vero sensu,; cf. , and 1, 573: haec duo tempora carent crimine,: carere omni malo mortem,: an ulla putatis Dona carere dolis Danaum?: nec lacrimis caruere genae,: pars quae peste caret,: oratio, quae astu caret,: oeconomia nomine Latino caret,: quae caret ora cruore nostro?: caret Ripa ventis,: aditu carentia saxa,: nivibus caritura Rhodope,: naturae vero rerum vis atque vis atque majestas in omnibus momentis fide caret,.—
To be deprived of, to be without, to feel the want of, to want something that is desirable: voluptate virtus saepe caret, nunquam indiget,: patriā,: quam huic erat miserum carere consuetudine amicorum, societate victus, sermone omnino familiari!: hac luce,: voluptatibus,: commodis omnibus,: provinciis atque oris Italiae maritimis ac portibus nostris,: tali munere,: citharā,: vate sacro,: patrio sepulcro,: libertate,: honore,: laude,: caret omni Majorum censu,has lost, dissipated,.—
With gen.: tui carendum quod erat,; so Laev. ap. .—
With acc.: quia Id quod amo careo,; cf. : eos parentes careo, Turp. ap. : DVLCEM. CARVI. LVCEM. CVM. TE. AMISI.,; so ; hence careri,pass.,; cf.: virque mihi dempto fine carendus abest,.—
With the access. idea of the subjective state of mind or feeling, to feel the want of a thing, to miss: triste enim est nomen ipsum carendi, quia subicitur haec vis; habuit, non habet; desiderat, requirit, indiget,; cf. the context: carere igitur hoc significat, egere eo quod habere velis, § 88: non caret is qui non desiderat,.

a distinguished philosopher of Cyrene, a pupil of the Stoic Diogenes, the founder of the New Academy in Athens, ; ; sq.; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—Hence,
Carnĕădēus or -dīus, a, um, adj., of Carneades: sententia,: divisio,: finis,: vis,

la:other:Carteia.html:
Cartēĭa, ae, f., = Καρτηία.
A very ancient seaport town in Hispania Baetica, now near Rocadillo, ; ; ; ; .—
Hence the adjj.,
Car-tēĭānus, a, um, Carteian, of Carteia: ora,.—
Cartēĭensis, e, the same: legati, Auct. B. Hisp. 36; absol., .—
The chief town of the Olcades, in Hispania Tarraconensis (acc. to others, Cartăla), ; cf. Alschefski ad h. l.

la:adj:carus.html:
cārus (not chārus; in Inscrr. often kārus, ; ), a, um, adj.
Sanscr. kan, to be beloved; kāru, agreeable
,
dear, precious, valued, esteemed (pass., freq. and class. in prose and poetry; syn.: dilectus, amatus, acceptus, gratus; opp. vilis, neglectus, contemptus; carum esse; syn. diligi); act., loving, affectionate, : carum ipsum verbum est amoris, ex quo amicitiae nomen est ductum,; ; ; : ego illum scio, quam carus sit cordi meo,; : neque meo cordi esse quemquam cariorem,: ut dis inmortalibus cari simus et ab iis diligamur,: dis carus ipsis,: laeta pax cariores Sabinas viris fecit,: populo carus atque jucundus,: patriae,; : parentes,: cari sunt parentes, cari liberi, propinqui, familiares: sed omnes omnium caritates patria una complexa est,: mater carissima, Asin. ap. .—So pater, ; : genitor,; : genitrix,: nutrix,: conjux,: Thisbe,: nata,: nepotes,: pignora, nati,; so also pignora, nepotes,; cf.: caput nepotis,: frater carissimus atque amantissimus,: homines mihi carissimi et amicissimi,: illa, quam Ego animo Egregie caram habuerim,; so, carum habere aliquem, (with amare); (with diligere): omnis suos caros habet, me quidem se ipso cariorem,: parentes carissimos habere,; ; : ex decessu carissimorum,: omnium societatum nulla est carior,: patria,: Athenae,: carmina legenti,crines,: simulacra,: amplexus, et saep.—Prov. uses: patria mihi vită meă multo est carior,; so ; cf. : carius oculis,; ; —Subst.: cārimei, my loved ones, —In a double sense with II., ; ; cf.: hoc est gratum nobisque est carius auro,.—
Prop. (opp. vilis), dear, costly, of a high price: venio ad macellum, rogito pisces: indicant Caros, agninam caram, caram bubulam, cara omnia,: quod ei amorem Carissimum... eum confeci sine sumptu,: quom cara annona sit,: coquos carissimus,.—So annona, ; ; (comp.) ; (sup.) et saep.: aurum argentumque caelando carius fecimus (cf. just before: auximus pretia rerum),, praef. 2, § 4; cf.: cariora pretia facere,.—With abl. pretii: quod non opus est, asse carum est. Cato ap. ; so, trecentis,.—Adv. (rare).
cārē.
Dearly, at a high price: vēnire,; comp., ; ;

sup., .—

Highly: carius aestimare, Plancus ap. .—
cārō (acc. to II.), dearly, at a high price, .

la:noun:caros.html:
cărŏs, i, m., = κάρος,
heavy sleep, torpor, sleep of death, .—
The seed of the hypericon, .

la:noun:carbo.html:
carbo, ōnis, m.
Sanscr. c)ra, coquere; cf. cremo
,
a coal, charcoal (dead or burning); of dead coals, ; ; ; —Of glowing, burning coals, ; ; ; ; , 18, § 82; 16, 10, 19, § 45; —
Meton.
From the black color of coals are derived the trop. expressions: impleantur elogiorum meae fores carbonibus,i.e. with scurrilous verses,: sanin cretā an carbone notati?; imitated by (cf. opp. albus): miror Proelia rubrica picta aut carbone,.—
For something of little value; hence prov.: carbonem pro thesauro invenire, to be deceived in one's expectation, .—
A bad tumor, ; cf. carbunculus, C.

la:noun:caritas.html:
cārĭtas, ātis, f.
carus
.
Prop., dearness, costliness, high price, etc. (opp. vilitas): annonae,; ; ; ; : rei frumentariae (opp. vilitas annonae),: nummorum,: olei,: vini,.—Also absol. caritas (sc. annonae), high prices, : ut tum vendas cum caritas est,: cum alter annus in vilitate, alter in summā caritate fuerit,; .—
Trop., regard, esteem, affection, love (cf. amor, I.; in good prose; syn.: benevolentia, favor, studium): cum deorum tum parentum patriaeque cultus eorumque hominum, qui aut sapientiā aut opibus excellunt, ad caritatem referri solet: conjuges autem et liberi, et fratres et alii, quos usus familiaritasque conjunxit, quamquam etiam caritate ipsā, tamen amore maxime continentur,; hence, opp. amor, as esteem to personal affection: si id videare, quod sit utile ipsis, defendere... haec res amorem magis conciliat, illa virtutis defensio caritatem,; cf. Treb. ap. ; : ut qui pacem belli amore turbaverant, bellum pacis caritate deponerent,: amor πάθος, caritas ἦθος, : caritas, quae est inter natos et parentes,; Quint. prooem. § 6: liberalitate qui utuntur benevolentiam sibi conciliant et caritatem,; ; : ingenita erga patriam caritas,: retinere caritatem in aliquem,: sanguine et caritate propior,: caritatem paraverat loco auctoritatis,— The subjoined gen. is usu. objective: patriae et suorum,; ; : rei publicae,; : domini,: Syracusanorum,: Hieronis,: liberum,: filiae,: ipsius soli,: sedium suarum,; .—But sometimes also subjective, love entertained by one: hominum, deorum,; : civium,; (with amor); or, more rarely, of the cause or ground of the love: caritas illius necessitudinis,: benevolentiae,.—In plur. of the different species of affection: omnes omnium caritates patria una complexa est,; : liberum,.—
In late Lat., meton., caritates = cari, the loved persons, ; .

la:noun:caria.html:
Cārĭa, ae, f., = Καρία.
A province in Asia Minor, south of Lydia, now the provinces Aïdin and Mentesche in Ejalet Anadoli, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; —
Hence,
Car, Cāris, a Carian, ; .—Orig., the supposed father of the Carian race, and inventor of augury by observing the fightof birds, .—And in plur.: Cāres, um, m., the inhabitants of Caria, the Carians, .—Acc. Gr. Cārăs, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; notorious for their treachery; hence the proverbial expression: quid? de totā Cariā nonne hoc vestrā voce vulgatum est, si quid cum periculo experiri velis, in Care id potissimum esse faciendum? Cic. l. l.—
Cārĭcus, a, um, Carian: creta,; .—Subst.: Cārĭca, ae (sc. ficus), a kind of dry fig, ; ; ; ; also for dried figs, in gen., ; ; .—
A town in Caria, called also Hydrela, .—
A harbor in Thrace, .

la:noun:carcer.html:
carcer, ĕris, m.
Sicilian κάρκαρον; cf. O. Müll. Etrusk. 1, p. 13; etym. dub.; cf. scrinium
,
an enclosed place; hence,
A prison, jail (syn.: custodia, vincula): si tresviri me in carcerem conpegerint,; ; ; ; : carcer, quem vindicem scelerum majores nostri esse voluerunt,.
Poet., of the custody of the winds, ; ; ; ; and of the lower world: carcer inferorum,: Ditis,.—Trop., of the chains of the body: qui ex corporum vinculis tamquam e carcere evolaverunt,; so ; .—
Esp., the Roman State-prison, close to the Forum, at the foot of the Capitoline Hill, on the right of the Sacra Via, built by Ancus Marcius, ; extended under ground by Servius Tullius; hence this part of the prison is called Tullianum. Bip.; ; ; ; ; cf.: in inferiorem demissus carcerem,: in carcerem conditi,; cf. also Müll., and Becker. Antiq. 1, 262 sq.; v. also Tullianum and robur, II. A.—
Meton.
The imprisoned criminals: in me carcerem effudistis,

.—

As a term of reproach ( = carcerarius), jail-bird, scapegallows: carcer vix carcere dignus, Lucil. ap. Don. ; l. l.—
The barrier or starting-place in the race-course (opp. meta or calx; v. h. vv.); usu. in plur., carceres, Müll.; ; ; ; ; * —In sing. (mostly poet.), ap. (v. 88 Vahl.); (imitated by ); ; ; Serv.; ; ; ; ; .—
Trop., the commencement, beginning, of a course of action or of a condition: a quibus carceribus decurrat ad metas,; so : ad carceres a calce revocari,i.e. to begin life anew,; cf.: cum aequalibus, quibus cum tamquam e carceribus emissus sis,.

senses: to tear off, tear out, rend, separate a whole into single parts, to cut to pieces, divide
to make good use of, enjoy something (usually a period of time)
of the effect of plucking: to tear or wear away or apart, pull to pieces, consume, waste
to revile, criticize, slander, carp at
la:verb:carpo.html:
carpo, psi, ptum, 3
cf.: rapio, ἁρπάζω, καρπος; Engl. grab, grip, grasp
.
Lit., of plants, flowers, fruits, etc., to pick, pluck, pluck off, cull, crop, gather (class.; in prose and poetry, esp. in the latter very freq.; syn. decerpere).
In gen.: (flos) tenui carptus ungui,; ; : ab arbore flores,; cf. infra, II.: rosam, poma,: violas et papavera,: violas, lilia,: frondes uncis manibus,: plenis pomaria ramis,: vindemiam de palmite,: fructus,: frumenta manu,.—
Esp.
Of animals, to take something as nourishment (cf. Burm. ad ); first, of nourishment from plants, to crop, pluck off, browse, graze on, etc. (syn. depascere); also of flesh, to eat, devour (rare): alia (animalia) sugunt, alia carpunt, alia vorant, alia mandunt,: carpunt gramen equi,; ; : herbam,; ; : pabula,; : alimenta,: apes carpunt ex oleā arbore ceram, e fico mel, etc.,gather,; cf.: apis carpens thyma,.—Poet.: Invidia (personif. envy) summa cacumina carpit,: nec carpsere jecur volucres,; cf. .—Sometimes transf., of men: prandium,: carpe cibos digitis,: pisces, pulles, .—Also, to carve; hence the pun in —
Poet., of other things, to tear off, tear away: summas carpens media inter cornua saetas,.—Of wool, to pluck; hence, poet., to spin: vellera,: pensa,; ; : lana carpta,carded, (hence, facete: stolidum pecus, to pluck, i. e. to fleece rich lovers, ; ): ex collo furtim coronas,to pull off,: crinem genasque,to tear, rend, lacerate,; so acc. to Servius's inaccurate account, in a fragment of the Twelve Tables: mulier faciem ne carpito, (instead of the real words: MVLIERES. GENAS. NE. RADVNTO.; cf. Dirks. Fragm. XII. Tab. p. 668): artus in parva frusta,.—
Trop.
(Acc. to I. A.) To pluck, snatch, etc.: ut omni ex genere orationem aucuper, et omnes undique flosculos carpam atque delibem,; : atque in legendo carpsi exinde quaedam,: oscula, to pluck, as it were, from the lips, to snatch, ; Loers. N. cr.; ; : basia,: gaudia,: dulcia,: regni commoda carpe mei,: fugitivaque gaudia carpe,and snatch pleasures as they fly,: delicias,—
Esp.
(Acc. to I. B. 1.) In a good sense, to enjoy, use, make use of (mostly poet.; syn.: fruor, capio): breve ver et primos carpere flores, (cf.: flore aetatis frui,): illa mihi sedes, illic mea carpitur aetas,spent, lived, passed,: diem,: honores virtutis,: auras vitales,; cf. : sub dio somnos,: quietem,: soporem,: noctes securas,; a poet. circumlocution for vivere, degere, etc.—
In a bad sense.
To gnaw at or tear character or reputation, to carp at, slander, calumniate, revile: more hominum invident, in conviviis rodunt, in circulis vellicant: non illo inimico, sed hoc maledico dente carpunt,: nam is carpebatur a Bibulo, Curione, Favonio,: Paulum obtrectatio carpsit,: imperatorem,: quae non desierunt carpere maligni,: maligno sermone,: obliquis orationibus,: nonnihil vocibus,: aliquem sermonibus,: sinistris sermonibus,: Ciceronem in his,: te ficto quaestu, and 37: et detorquere recte facta,: famam vitamque,; .—
To rob of strength, to weaken, enfeeble, wear away, consume; or poet., with the idea extended (cf. absumo), to consume completely, to destroy: vires,; : quid si carpere singula (jura) et extorquere... patiemini,; esp. of in ward care, anxiety, longing, etc.: at regina, gravi jamdudum saucia curā, Volnus alit venis et caeco carpitur igni,; ; : solane perpetua maerens carpere juventā?: curā carpitur ista mei,: aegra assiduo mens carpitur aestu,; ; : invidia carpit et carpitur unā,; cf. . non ego Tot tuos patiar labores carpere lividas Obliviones,to wear away,; cf.: otia corpus alunt, animus quoque pascitur illis; Inmodicus contra carpit utrumque labor,: aras etiam templaque demolitur et obscurat oblivio, neglegit carpitque posteritas,: totum potest excedere quod potest carpi,.—So,
In milit. lang., to inflict injury upon an enemy (esp. by single, repeated attacks), to weaken, harass: agmen adversariorum,: hostes carpere multifariam vires Romanas,; ; ; cf. infra; Weissenb. ad ; ; : novissimum agmen,: novissimos,: extrema agminis,. —
To separate a whole into single parts, to cut to pieces, divide (syn.: dividere, distribuere): neque semper utendum est perpetuitate, sed saepe carpenda membris minutioribus

oratio est, : in multas parvasque partes carpere exercitum,: summam unius belli in multa proelia parvaque,: Erymanthus... ab accolis rigantibus carpitur,is drawn off into canals,. —With a reference to the meaning

supra: si erunt plures qui ob innocentem condemnandum pecuniam acceperint, tu non animadvertes in omnis, sed carpes ut velis, et paucos ex multis ad ignominiam sortiere?distinguish, single out,; cf.: in multorum peccato carpi paucos ad ignominiam,—
Viam, iter, etc., or with definite local substantives, terram, mare, litora, etc., to go, tread upon, pass over, navigate, sail along or through, to take or pursue one's way (syn. ire): viam,; ; ; : iter,; ; ; : supremum iter = mori,: gyrum,to go in a circle,: fugam,to fly,; cf.: prata fugā,: pede viam,: pede iter,: pedibus terras, pontum remis,: pede campos,: mare,: litora,; 15, 507: aëra alis,; cf. : aethera,: carpitur acclivis per muta silentia trames,.

senses: hinge (of a door or gate), usually a pivot and socket in Roman times.
A street, that ran north–south, in a Roman town or military camp
turning point, critical moment or action
the symbolism of the hinge in ancient Roman religion and myth
la:noun:cardo.html:
cardo, ĭnis, m.
cf. κράδη, a swing; κραδαίνω, to swing, wave; Sanscr. kurd, a spring, a leap; old Germ. hrad, lively, and Germ. reit in bereit, ready
(f., Gracch. ap. P.; Graius ap. ; cf. infra in Vitr.),
the pivot and socket, upon which a door was made to swing at the lintel and the threshold, the hinge of a door or gate, Vahl.: paene ecfregisti foribus cardines,; : postis a cardine vellit Aeratos,: cardo stridebat,; cf. : num muttit cardo?: immoti,: singuli,: facili patuerunt cardine valvae,: versato cardine Thisbe Egreditur,opening the door,; cf. : nec strepitum verso Saturnia cardine fecit,—
Meton.
Cardines, in mechanics, beams that were fitted together; and specifically, cardo masculus, a tenon, , and cardo femina, a socket, a mortise, : cardo securiclatus,axeshaped tenon, a dovetail,.— Hence,
In garlands, the place where the two ends meet, .—
In astron., the point about which something turns, a pole. So of the North pole: caeli,: mundi,; cf.: extremusque adeo duplici de cardine vertex Dicitur esse polus, Cic. poët. N. D. 2, 41, 105; ; : cardo glacialis ursae,: Arctoae cardo portae,; hence anal. to this, with the agrimensores,the line limiting the field, drawn through from north to south,; ; cf. Fest. s. v. decimanus, p. 71 Müll., and accordingly the mountain Taurus is called cardo, i. e. line or limit, ; cf. ; .—Of the four cardinal points of the world, ; so, Hesperius Eous, ; : occiduus,: medius,.— Of the earth as the centre of the universe, acc. to the belief of the ancients, ; .—Of the intersection of inclined surfaces: reperiuntur (aquae) ... quodam convexitatis cardine aut montium radicibus,.—Of the summer solstice: anni,; and so of the epochs of the different seasons: temporum,; .—Hence, of the time of life: extremus,old age,.—
Trop., that on which every thing else turns or depends, the chief point or circumstance (so not before the Aug. per.): haud tanto cessabit cardine rerum,at such a turn of affairs, so great a crisis, in so critical a moment, decisive, (hoc est in articulo, Serv.; cf. ; Gr. ἀκμἧ): fatorum in cardine summo,: litium. : causae,: satellitem in quo totius dominationis summa quasi quodam cardine continetur,, ext. 5: unum eligamus in quo est summum ac principale, in quo totius sapientiae cardo versatur,.

la:other:Caria.html:
Cārĭa, ae, f., = Καρία.
A province in Asia Minor, south of Lydia, now the provinces Aïdin and Mentesche in Ejalet Anadoli, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; —
Hence,
Car, Cāris, a Carian, ; .—Orig., the supposed father of the Carian race, and inventor of augury by observing the fightof birds, .—And in plur.: Cāres, um, m., the inhabitants of Caria, the Carians, .—Acc. Gr. Cārăs, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; notorious for their treachery; hence the proverbial expression: quid? de totā Cariā nonne hoc vestrā voce vulgatum est, si quid cum periculo experiri velis, in Care id potissimum esse faciendum? Cic. l. l.—
Cārĭcus, a, um, Carian: creta,; .—Subst.: Cārĭca, ae (sc. ficus), a kind of dry fig, ; ; ; ; also for dried figs, in gen., ; ; .—
A town in Caria, called also Hydrela, .—
A harbor in Thrace, .

la:noun:carnificina.html:
carnĭfĭcīna (carnŭf-), ae. f.
carnifex
.
The office of executioner or hangman; capital punishment, execution: carnificinam facere = carnificem esse,; cf. : locus carnificinae,.—Hence,
Per meton., the rack, torture, torment: dolores atque carnificinas facere, Cato ap. ; and ap. ; so, carnificinam subire,: in ergastulum et carnificinam duci,.—
Trop.: cum omnis perturbatio miseria est, tum carnificina est aegritudo,; cf. (= crudelitas).
